content: The Fallopian tubes, also referred to as oviducts, uterine tubes, or salpinges (singular: salpinx), are two delicate tubular structures that connect the ovaries to the uterus in female mammals. These tubes are not directly attached to the ovaries but open into the peritoneal cavity, which is the internal space of the abdomen. This anatomical arrangement creates a direct communication pathway between the peritoneal cavity and the external environment via the vagina. In humans, the Fallopian tubes are approximately 7 to 14 cm in length. Anatomy There are two Fallopian tubes, each attached to one side of the uterine cornua (the upper corners of the uterus) and terminating near an ovary. The terminal end of each tube forms a structure called the fimbria, which helps guide the ovum into the tube. Despite their proximity, the Fallopian tubes are not physically connected to the ovaries. Regions The Fallopian tube is divided into four distinct regions, progressing from the ovary to the uterus: 1. Infundibulum: This region contains the fimbriae, which are finger-like projections that help capture the ovum. 2. Ampulla: This is the widest section of the tube and is the most common site of fertilization. 3. Isthmus: A narrower segment that connects the ampulla to the uterus. 4. Intramural portion: This part passes through the uterine wall and opens into the uterine cavity. Histology The Fallopian tube is composed of three layers: 1. Mucosa: The innermost layer, characterized by distinctive folds. These folds contain ciliated cells and peg cells. The cilia help propel the ovum toward the uterus, while peg cells secrete nutrients. The complexity of the mucosal folds varies by region, being most elaborate in the ampulla and nearly absent in the intramural portion. 2. Muscularis externa: The middle layer, composed of smooth muscle, facilitates peristaltic movements. 3. Serosa: The outermost layer, which is a thin protective covering. Motility The Fallopian tubes are highly mobile structures. Time-lapse videography has shown that they move dynamically within the pelvis. Contrary to static anatomical illustrations, the tubes do not remain fixed in position throughout the menstrual cycle. They may cross over to the opposite side or rest on top of the uterus. Function in Fertilization When an ovum matures within an ovarian follicle, the follicle and the ovarian wall rupture, releasing the ovum into the peritoneal cavity. The fimbriae of the Fallopian tube guide the ovum into the tube, where it begins its journey toward the uterus. This movement is facilitated by the coordinated action of cilia lining the tube. The journey can take several hours to days. If fertilization occurs within the ampulla, the resulting zygote typically implants in the uterine endometrium, initiating pregnancy. However, in some cases, the embryo implants within the Fallopian tube itself, leading to an ectopic pregnancy, commonly referred to as a tubal pregnancy. Embryology and Homology The Fallopian tubes develop from the Müllerian ducts during embryogenesis. In females, the Müllerian ducts give rise to the Fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper portion of the vagina. In males, the corresponding Wolffian ducts develop into structures such as the epididymis and vas deferens. The Fallopian tubes are not homologous to any male reproductive structures. Pathology The Fallopian tubes can be affected by pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which may lead to obstruction of the tubes. This can result in infertility or an increased risk of ectopic pregnancy. Surgery The surgical removal of a Fallopian tube is termed a salpingectomy, while the removal of both tubes is called a bilateral salpingectomy. If the procedure involves the removal of a Fallopian tube along with at least one ovary, it is referred to as a salpingo-oophorectomy. Surgical restoration of a blocked Fallopian tube is known as tuboplasty. Etymology and Nomenclature The Fallopian tubes are named after Gabriele Falloppio, a 16th-century Italian anatomist who first described them. Although the term Fallopian tube is eponymous, some texts use a lowercase f to reflect its integration into modern English as a standard anatomical term. The Greek word salpinx (σάλπιγξ), meaning trumpet, is also used to describe these structures. Additional Images Various anatomical illustrations depict the Fallopian tubes in relation to the uterus, ovaries, and surrounding pelvic structures. These include sectional views of the gravid uterus, the broad ligament, and the internal reproductive anatomy of females.
